vignette:
She is 40, European, married, and works as a data scientist, a job she once loved for its orderliness. Before the trauma, she describes herself as someone who found comfort in patterns: clean datasets, solvable problems, forecasts that could be improved if she just looked closely enough. She and her husband had a steady life, quietly satisfying, with routines that suited them both. She took the train to work, stopped for coffee at the same place most mornings, and liked the feeling that the day could be anticipated.

The event that divides her life into “before” and “after” happens on an ordinary weekday evening. She is leaving the station, distracted by a work message on her phone, when she hears shouting and then a sound she still struggles to name without her throat tightening. A man several feet ahead of her is struck in a violent assault. She does not know him. What stays with her is not a coherent sequence but fragments: the angle of his body hitting the pavement, a woman screaming, a shoe lying in the road, blood spreading in a way her mind still insists on replaying in slowed detail. She remembers freezing. She thinks she should have done more, moved faster, shouted louder, something. Instead she stands there for what feels like a long time, though she knows it may only have been seconds, until others rush in and emergency services arrive.

That night, she does not sleep. Each time she closes her eyes, the scene returns with startling vividness, as if her mind is determined to force her back there. In the first weeks, she tells herself she is simply shaken. She goes back to work quickly, wanting proof that life is normal. But normal no longer feels available to her. On the train, she scans every carriage for signs of danger. At the station, her chest tightens and her pace changes without her deciding to speed up. If she hears raised voices, her body reacts first: shoulders locked, heart pounding, breath held high in her chest.

At work, she tries to disappear into code and models, but concentration has become unreliable. She opens the same file three times and cannot remember what she intended to do. She stares at data visualizations and finds herself seeing the shape of blood on concrete. Meetings are worse than solitary tasks. If a colleague speaks abruptly, she startles. If someone stands behind her chair unexpectedly, she jolts so visibly that people apologize, and then she feels ashamed. She used to be precise and patient with junior team members; now she finds herself irritable, wanting people to stop asking her questions she would once have welcomed.

Her husband notices first that she is no longer sleeping through the night. She thrashes, wakes gasping, and sometimes sits upright, confused about where she is. He reaches for her and she recoils before she recognizes him. She hates that moment. During the day she becomes preoccupied with safety in ways that feel both excessive and impossible to control. She checks locks repeatedly. She texts him to confirm he has arrived places safely. She studies strangers’ hands, posture, tone, trying to calculate threat from ordinary human behavior. As someone who works professionally with probabilities and prediction, she is tormented by how useless those skills feel in the face of random violence. She keeps thinking that if she had been more observant, she could have anticipated what happened. Intellectually, she knows this is unlikely. Emotionally, she remains unconvinced.

Over time, her world contracts. She changes her commute to avoid the station where the assault occurred, even though the alternative adds nearly an hour to her day. Then she begins working from home more often, telling colleagues it helps her productivity. She stops meeting friends in busy public places. Restaurants with outdoor seating feel exposed; crowded streets feel unbearable. When her husband suggests a weekend trip, she invents reasons not to go. She says she is tired, overloaded, behind on a project. The truth is that being away from the small set of controlled spaces she trusts feels impossible.

What troubles her most is the sense that part of her remains stuck in that evening. She can be sitting at her kitchen table with her laptop open, sunlight on the floor, her husband in the next room, and suddenly she is back at the station, hearing the scream and seeing the man fall. In those moments, her body behaves as if the danger is present now. Afterward she feels wrung out, embarrassed, and strangely alone. She avoids news reports about assaults but cannot stop herself from reading them when they appear. She tells herself she is looking for closure, for information, for some final piece that will let her mind file the event away. Instead, each detail seems to sharpen the memory.

She speaks quietly about how much smaller her life has become. She still performs well enough at work that others assume she is managing. From the outside, she remains competent, analytical, reliable. Inside, she feels watchful, brittle, and exhausted, as though her mind no longer belongs fully to the present but is organized around preventing a terrible moment that has already happened.
